newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan big banks seen returning to black in 96/97.
newsitem.headline: Japan big banks seen returning to black in 96/97.

text.p: Falling stock prices and financial failures have battered the balance sheets of Japan's leading banks but most will manage to eke out a reasonable profit for the just-ended business year, analysts say.

Hurt by the sinking stock market, bad loan disposals and the repercussions of problems at smaller financial firms, the banks have had to struggle to land in the black for 1996/97 after mostly posting losses the previous year.

Among the 20 top banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB), Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB) and Nippon Trust Bank recently revised their business forecasts for 1996/97, which ended on March 31, to predict parent current losses rather than profits.
But the rest have predicted profits, albeit on a more modest scale than they had originally expected.
The nation's top 10 commercial banks are scheduled to announce 1996/97 business results on May 23. Seven major trust banks and three long-term credit banks will do so on May 26.

"Many of the top banks will likely have struggled to post profits last business year," said Katsuhito Sasajima, an analyst at Nikko Research Center. "Their operating profits were better than expected but they had to continue disposing of big problem loans and mark down appraisal losses on shareholdings."
A downswing in Tokyo's stock market dealt a blow to earnings, forcing them to take appraisal losses on shareholdings whose market price was below the book value as of the end of the business year.

But the damage could have been worse. The key Nikkei average recovered to end the business year at 18,003 after hitting a low of 17,303 in January. But the closing level was still much lower than 21,406 at the end of 1995/96.

The total of the 20 banks' own forecasts for parent operating profits for the past fiscal year is 4.4 trillion yen ($36.9 billion), compared with a previous aggregate forecast of 4.0 trillion yen ($33.6 billion) based on the banks' November forecasts, and an actual 4.8 trillion yen ($40.3 billion) in 1995/96. Analysts said they would likely match the target.

Operating profits in 1995/96 were exceptionally good thanks to falling interest rates, and a further fall in rates in the latter half of 1996/97 also contributed to better-than-expected operating profits, which are pretax profits from banking business.

Analysts also estimate the 20 banks disposed of 6.0 trillion yen ($50.4 billion) of problem loans in 1996/97. This was lower than the 10.8 trillion yen ($90.7 billion) of disposals a year earlier but was higher than had been expected.

London-based credit rating agency IBCA said the bigger problem loan write-offs reflected a continued fall in land prices and earlier-than-expected moves to clear up problems stemming from links with other financial firms.

In particular, many banks wrote off problem loans stemming from the failure of three financial firms affiliated with Nippon Credit Bank (NCB) in early April, it said. On April 1, NCB announced a restructuring under which it withdrew support for the affiliates.
On the same day, Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Japan's 10th biggest commercial bank, announced a merger with regional Hokkaido Bank Ltd to try to improve its financial health.
On a parent current basis, large losses at just a few banks are expected to drag down aggregate earnings for the top 20 to a loss of 108 billion yen ($907 million) in 1996/97.
Current earnings include gains or losses from securities holdings.
Analysts estimate that to cover stock appraisal losses and actively dispose of problem loans, the 20 banks raised some 1.2 trillion yen ($10 billion) through stock sales in 1996/97.
Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan, said he thought many of the top banks had already cut problem loans to manageable levels after active write-offs in past years.

The banks operating profits could slip below four trillion yen ($33.6 billion) in 1997/98, as interest rates are expected to rise, but the amount of write-offs will probably fall to about four trillion yen ($33.6 billion), he said.
Nikko's Sasajima was more cautious, however. "Problem loans may rise further if the economic recovery slows, and lower stock prices may force banks to mark down appraisal losses again," he said.
